# PostMortem AI — full reference

Canonical product: [https://www.nanoneuron.ai/](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/)
[Short index](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/llms.txt)
[Docs](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/docs)

[Two Cloudflare outages, in postmortem form](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/blog/cloudflare-outages-2025) (the template filled from Cloudflare's own reports, every line quoted verbatim -- assembled by hand, not tool output)
[GitHub outage demo](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/blog/github-outage-demo) (the tool's own unedited output on a real public incident)
[Published postmortems](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/postmortems)
[Pricing](https://www.nanoneuron.ai/pricing)

Contact: vish.matale@gmail.com
Last factual review: 2026-09-12

This file is the complete reference; llms.txt above is the short index. Every
claim here is checked against the running code and, where practical, against
live production behavior as of the review date — not a roadmap or an
aspirational description. If this file and the running product ever disagree,
the running product is correct and this file is stale.

## What this is

A single-account incident postmortem tool for DevOps and SRE teams, and for
freelance SRE/DevOps consultants working a single client engagement: record
evidence about an incident as it unfolds, generate an AI-drafted postmortem
grounded in that evidence, publish it once a named human approves. Each
account is one person's own incidents — no shared organizations, teams, or
roles yet, so a freelancer serving multiple clients is one account per
engagement today, not built-in multi-client management.

## Architecture

- Backend: FastAPI (Python), deployed as a Vercel serverless function.
- Frontend: Next.js App Router (React), deployed to Vercel.
- Database: PostgreSQL (Supabase), accessed via a connection pool; pooled
  (`:6543`) connections disable server-side prepared statements to avoid a
  transaction-pooler incompatibility.
- AI: Gemini (`gemini-2.5-flash` by default for drafting/extraction,
  configurable via `GEMINI_MODEL`; `gemini-embedding-001`
  for RAG embeddings at 768 dimensions, matching the `vector(768)` column).
  Claude is a real, configured fallback provider (not just described), used
  only when Gemini's own call fails or its circuit breaker is open — each
  provider has its own independent circuit breaker (closed/open/half-open).
- 29 forward-only SQL migrations as of this review.

## The core guarantee: grounded drafting

Two independent layers, not one unsupervised model call:

1. The drafting model receives the incident's evidence entries, numbered, and
   is instructed (system prompt, verbatim rules): every claim must cite an
   entry number; an unsupported section should be left empty/uncited rather
   than inferred; never estimate cost, revenue, or customer counts not stated
   in the evidence; never invent dates, deadlines, or names; never recommend
   an action the evidence doesn't support; retrieved similar past incidents
   (RAG, below) are reference-only and must never be cited.
2. Code — not a second model call — independently re-verifies every citation
   against the real evidence list before anything is persisted. An invalid
   citation (missing, out of range, wrong type) causes that claim to be
   replaced with the fixed marker `"Not established by the recorded
   evidence."` for the four required sections (summary, root_cause,
   detection, resolution), or dropped entirely for optional lists
   (contributing_factors, actions). This step can only remove or replace the
   model's own text — it has no path to add new text of its own.

Verified live, deliberately adversarially, not just on the happy path: a
draft built from genuinely vague evidence ("things felt slow... got better
later") correctly returned the literal `root_cause` marker rather than
inventing a cause, and every other field stayed strictly within the vague
language actually given — no fabricated numbers, dates, or causes. Drafting
with zero evidence entries is refused outright (409) rather than attempted.

Publishing requires a named human approval; `incident_postmortems` has a
database `CHECK` constraint that a row cannot be marked `published` without
both `approved_by` and `approved_at` set — enforced at the schema level, not
just by application code or a UI convention.

## RAG (similar past incidents)

When drafting, the account's own previously *published* postmortems that are
semantically similar to the current incident are retrieved via cosine
similarity over embeddings and shown to the model as labeled reference
context — never numbered, never citable. The citation-verification step only
ever checks against the current incident's own numbered evidence, so a
retrieved past incident structurally cannot become the source for a claim,
regardless of what the model outputs.

## Evidence model

Each evidence entry has: `source` (a fixed type category — `alert`, `log`,
`deploy`, `metric`, `human_note`, or `customer_report`; not a vendor/tool
name), `summary` (required), `detail` (optional), `occurred_at` (epoch
milliseconds), and is attributed to whoever/whatever recorded it (a signed-in
user, or `"webhook"` for automated ingestion). Incidents have a `severity` of
`sev1`–`sev4` and a `status` of `open`/`resolved`.

## Webhook ingestion

Every account has a real, rotatable per-account token
(`GET /v1/webhooks/token`, `POST /v1/webhooks/token/rotate` — rotating
immediately invalidates every URL built with the old token). Posting to
`/v1/webhooks/incidents/{token}` either appends to an existing open incident
(if `incident_id` is given and belongs to the caller) or creates a new one —
the same write path and paywall as the authenticated app, just authenticated
by token instead of session cookie. Rate-limited to 100 events/hour per
account. Generic, source-agnostic — put the sending tool's name in
`summary`/`detail`. An optional `resolved: true` on an event appending to
an existing incident auto-transitions it to resolved, matching the
resolved-event most real monitoring tools already send — one-directional
only (never reopens a resolved incident) and only takes effect when
appending to an existing incident, never on creation.

`POST /v1/webhooks/pagerduty/{token}` is a second, PagerDuty-specific
adapter over the same underlying write path (both routes share one
`_ingest_event()` — the paywall check, rate limit, and evidence insert are
never duplicated). It parses PagerDuty's real v3 webhook envelope
(`event.event_type`, `event.data.id/title/urgency/html_url`) directly:
`incident.triggered` creates an incident and stores PagerDuty's own
incident id as `incidents.external_id` (migration 0025); a later
`incident.resolved` for the same PagerDuty incident id finds that same
row by `external_id` and resolves it, since PagerDuty has no way to be
told this app's own incident id back. Urgency (`high`/`low`, PagerDuty's
only two levels) maps conservatively to `sev2`/`sev4`. Any other event
type gets a 200 with `{"status": "ignored"}` rather than an error —
PagerDuty disables a subscription after enough non-2xx responses, and
there's no per-event-type filter in its own subscription config.
Datadog has no adapter route: its webhook payload is entirely
user-templated on Datadog's side, so its "integration" is a documented
JSON template (account settings) for Datadog's own webhook payload field,
pointed at the generic endpoint above — there is no fixed Datadog schema
to parse.

`POST /v1/webhooks/slack/{token}` is a Slack Events API receiver over the
same `_ingest_event()` write path — paste it as a Slack app's Event
Subscriptions Request URL, subscribe to `message.channels`, invite the app
to an incident channel, and the channel records itself as the incident
unfolds instead of being pasted in afterwards. **A Slack thread maps to one
incident**: `external_id` is `slack:{channel}:{thread_root_ts}`, so the
first message opens an incident and every reply appends evidence to that
same one, via the identical `external_id` lookup PagerDuty uses. A message
outside a thread keys on its own `ts`, so unrelated channel chatter is
never absorbed into someone else's incident. Slack's one-time
`url_verification` challenge is answered before the token lookup, since it
carries no account context.

Three refusals in that route are deliberate, not omissions. **Bot messages
are dropped** — this app posts its own notifications *into* Slack via the
outbound `slack_webhook_url` integration, so ingesting bot output would feed
those back as evidence and the product would cite text it wrote itself.
**Edits and deletions are ignored** (`message_changed`, `message_deleted`) —
evidence is append-only and provenance-preserving, so a later edit must not
rewrite a row already cited. **Nothing auto-resolves from chat** — someone
typing "we're resolved" is not an authenticated state change, unlike a
PagerDuty resolve, which is a real transition in a system of record and does
auto-draft. Evidence lands with `source: human_note`, one of the six values
`incident_evidence`'s CHECK constraint permits. Unrecognised payloads return
an ignored 200, since Slack disables a subscription that keeps failing.
Authentication is the URL token only, like the other webhook routes.

## Similar-incident retrieval, evidence quality, and draft comparison

`GET /incidents/{id}/similar` runs the same account-scoped, published-only
similarity search drafting already uses internally as hidden RAG context,
reachable directly so a human can see "3 incidents like this before" ahead
of drafting, not just have it invisibly shape the model's output.
`GET /quality-summary` aggregates how often each of the four required
sections came back as the fixed unsupported marker across the account's
own drafts — a pattern-level signal about evidence habits, not a
judgment on any single draft. `GET /incidents/{id}/previous-draft`
returns the snapshot taken immediately before the most recent re-draft
overwrote it (`postmortem_draft_history`, append-only), so a re-draft is
comparable to what it replaced instead of an unexplained rewrite.

## MCP

The backend exposes a real MCP server (`/mcp` on the API; federated to
`/api/mcp` on the frontend under the caller's own session), 15 tools
total: founder-only (`get_founder_summary`, `list_payment_claims`,
`approve_payment_claim`, `reject_payment_claim`, `run_read_only_sql` — a
defense-in-depth read-only query tool, `list_agent_activity` — the
cross-account activity-log query below) and client-scoped
(`list_incidents`, `get_dashboard_summary`, `create_incident`,
`add_evidence`, `draft_postmortem`, `find_similar_incidents`,
`publish_postmortem`, `get_integrations`, `update_integrations`) — the
same business logic and authorization as the REST endpoints below, not a
parallel implementation.

## Agent accountability

Every MCP tool call is recorded into `account_activity_log` (the same
table REST-driven actions already wrote into, tagged `source='web'` vs.
`source='mcp_agent'`), including denials: a `PermissionError` raised by
one of the three subscription/founder gates above is caught and logged as
a denial before propagating, so a blocked attempt is visible, not just a
successful one. Reads and writes are split into an explicit command
(`RecordActivityCommand`/`handle_record_activity`) and query
(`ActivityLogFilter`/`handle_activity_log_query`, real keyset pagination
on `(created_at, id)`, not `OFFSET`) in `app/cqrs/activity.py`, shared by
every reader: `GET /v1/postmortems/activity-log` (caller's own account),
`GET /v1/founder/activity-log` (every account, filterable by
client_email/source/time window), and the `list_agent_activity` MCP tool
above -- one query implementation behind all three, not three that could
drift apart.

## REST API surface (all under `/v1`)

Airlock (`/v1/airlock`): `POST /waitlist` (public; records an early-access
signup, answers 202 identically whether the address is new or already on the
list so the response cannot be used to enumerate it; per-IP limited),
`GET /waitlist` (founder-only; the list itself). There is no scan endpoint on
this API -- see "Airlock" below for why.

Auth (`/v1/auth`): `POST /register`, `POST /login`, `POST /logout`,
`GET /me`, `PUT /me`, `PATCH /me`, `DELETE /me` (founder account cannot
self-delete), `POST /password-reset/request`, `POST /password-reset/confirm`,
`GET /captcha-config`, `GET /session-token`.

Incidents & postmortems (`/v1/postmortems`): `POST /incidents/suggest`
(AI-suggested title + severity from pasted raw text, for the create form to
pre-fill -- suggestion only, creates nothing), `POST /incidents`,
`GET /incidents`, `GET /incidents/{id}`, `PATCH /incidents/{id}/status`,
`GET /summary`, `POST /incidents/{id}/evidence`,
`GET /incidents/{id}/evidence`, `POST /incidents/{id}/evidence/extract`
(AI-assisted extraction from pasted raw text), `POST /incidents/{id}/draft`,
`POST /incidents/{id}/publish`, `PATCH /incidents/{id}/public`,
`GET /incidents/{id}/postmortem.md` (the postmortem as a Markdown file in the
same shape as /postmortem-template: evidence numbered, every citation
resolved to a number, the dropped-claim count included),
`PATCH /incidents/{id}/actions/{action_id}` (follow-up tracking: move a
drafted action item through open / in_progress / done / dropped; `GET
/summary` reports `open_actions` still owed across all incidents),
`GET /public` (list published+public postmortems), `GET /public/{slug}`,
`GET /export` (the caller's own full data as JSON), `GET /activity-log`
(the caller's own account_activity_log rows, source-tagged web vs.
mcp_agent -- see Agent accountability above).

Billing (`/v1/billing`): `POST /checkout`, `POST /portal`, `GET /status`,
`GET /card/pricing`, `POST /webhook` (Stripe, signature-verified),
`GET /upi/pricing` (public), `GET /upi/info` (founder-only — the real UPI
ID is never returned in an API response to a client account),
`POST /upi/email-details` (self-serve: emails the real UPI ID to the
caller's own registered address, no founder round-trip needed),
`POST /upi/claim`, `GET /upi/claims`, `GET /wire/pricing` (public),
`GET /wire/info` (founder-only, same reasoning as UPI),
`POST /wire/email-details` (self-serve, same as UPI above),
`POST /wire/claim`, `GET /wire/claims`, `PATCH /claims/{id}` (edit a
still-pending claim's reference), `DELETE /claims/{id}` (withdraw a
still-pending claim), `POST /bank-alert` (inbound webhook for a forwarded
real bank credit alert — verifies a claim's reference against a real bank
alert but never itself grants access; only a founder's explicit approval
does that).

Webhooks (`/v1/webhooks`): `GET /token`, `POST /token/rotate`,
`POST /incidents/{token}`.

Integrations (`/v1/integrations`): `GET ""`, `PUT ""` (Slack webhook URL,
Linear API key/team ID — best-effort notifications on publish, never block
the publish response on failure).

Founder-only (`/v1/founder`): `GET /summary`, `GET /payment-claims`,
`POST /payment-claims/{id}/approve`, `POST /payment-claims/{id}/reject`,
`POST /payment-claims/{id}/annotate`, `GET /payment-claims/{id}/events`,
`GET /activity-log` (every account's activity, not just the caller's own
— filterable by `client_email`, `source`, `since_ms`/`until_ms`, keyset
`cursor`-paginated; see Agent accountability above).

## Auth model

Session cookie, HMAC-signed. `current_user` (401 if absent/invalid) vs
`current_founder` (403 if signed in but not the configured founder email) are
distinct dependencies — a request with no session gets 401; a real, signed-in
non-founder account hitting a founder-only route gets 403. Login is
rate-limited per account and per IP; registration and password-reset requests
are separately rate-limited by IP; drafting and incident creation are
rate-limited per account (the AI-cost-incurring actions). Registration/login
can require a Cloudflare Turnstile CAPTCHA when configured. Login and
password-reset both give an identical, generic failure message regardless of
whether the account exists — deliberately, to prevent account enumeration.

## Payments

Creating an incident, evidence, AI extraction, drafting, publishing, and
creating a second incident all require an active subscription.

**Price.** One plan, no tiers. India: ₹999/month or ₹9,990/year via UPI.
International: USD 15, GBP 12, or EUR 14 per month, or USD 150, GBP 120, or
EUR 140 per year, via SWIFT wire. Annual is charged for ten months, so two
months are free (`ANNUAL_MONTHS_CHARGED`, default 10). Live prices are served
publicly and unauthenticated from `GET /v1/billing/upi/pricing`
(`amount_inr`, `amount_inr_annual`) and `GET /v1/billing/wire/pricing`
(per-currency `amount`, `amount_annual`) — those endpoints, not this
document, are the authority if the two ever disagree.

**Annual is the recommended option for international customers, and not as a
discount.** A SWIFT wire costs the sender roughly USD 15–40 in bank fees.
Against a USD 15 monthly subscription that is a surcharge larger than the
product itself, every month, so monthly-by-wire is not economically sensible;
annual makes it a one-off cost on a single larger transfer. The billing
period is stored on the claim (`payment_claims.billing_period`, migration
0029, constrained to `monthly`/`annual`) rather than inferred from the
amount, because an amount alone is ambiguous across currencies and approval
needs to know unambiguously how long a grant should last.

For clients in any country, two real paths work today: (1)
manual UPI (India), founder-reviewed; (2) manual international SWIFT wire
(USD/GBP/EUR), founder-reviewed. Both are self-serve to get started: a
signed-in client requests the real account details (UPI ID; wire account
number, SWIFT code, correspondent bank) via `POST /upi/email-details` or
`POST /wire/email-details`, which emails them to that client's own
registered address -- no founder round-trip needed just to find out how
to pay. Submitting the transaction reference afterward still requires the
founder's explicit approval before access activates. Indian-diaspora customers are not limited to wire: an NRI with an
NRE/NRO account and an international mobile number (US, UK, Canada,
Australia, Singapore, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Malaysia,
Hong Kong, France) can pay via UPI in INR instead, instantly and
with none of the correspondent-bank fees a wire incurs. The wire
payment-details email says so explicitly.
A third path — Stripe Checkout,
self-serve, instant activation on webhook receipt, cancel/manage via the
Stripe Customer Portal — is fully built and code-complete but not yet
switched on for real payments (the production Stripe key is currently
test-mode; `card_pricing`'s own `configured` check requires a live-mode
key, confirmed by inspecting a real live checkout session before that
check existed). It will appear as an option automatically once live keys
are set, with no other change needed. Manual claims are matched to real
bank alerts
automatically (verification only — a founder's explicit approval is the only
thing that ever activates access, regardless of automated verification).
Every real payment endpoint verifies against the provider's own record
(amount, currency, signature, captured status), never against
frontend-supplied state.

**Every account gets one free incident.** Record evidence on it, generate a
grounded draft, and see the real output before paying anything. A subscription
is required to create a *second* incident and to publish. The allowance is
enforced in one place (`has_free_incident_available` in `apps/api/app/auth.py`)
and honoured identically by the REST API, the MCP tools and the webhook
ingestion path, so it cannot be bypassed by choosing a different entry point.
This trial was switched off on 2026-09-04 and restored on 2026-09-10 after the
evidence was clear: every payment taken to that point was made while the free
incident existed, and none afterwards. An account that drafted a real
postmortem on its free incident and never subscribed receives exactly one
automated reminder email, at least 24 hours after that draft — a plain link to
pricing, never a repeat send and never a fabricated urgency claim.
Refunds: email vish.matale@gmail.com within 14 days of the first charge
and it's refunded — a manual, founder-processed action on every payment
rail, the same review discipline as approving a payment in the first
place. No self-serve automated refund endpoint exists — deliberately:
this app's whole identity is that consequential actions need a human,
not inferred approval, and an automated outbound-money action would be
the same thing in reverse.

## What this doesn't do

- Auto-publish anything — always a deliberate, named human action.
- Estimate cost, revenue, or customer-impact figures the evidence didn't
  state — the system prompt explicitly forbids it.
- Vendor-specific webhook parsing beyond PagerDuty (real adapter) and
  Datadog (documented payload template) — any other monitoring tool
  still works via the generic, un-adapted webhook endpoint.
- Support multiple people, teams, or roles on one account.
- Claim any measured quality score, uptime percentage, or customer count
  that hasn't actually been measured — this file states architecture and
  verified behavior, not marketing figures.

## Access & discovery

Public marketing/docs/published-postmortem pages are meant to be indexed;
every account-scoped page requires authentication and is not meant to be
crawled as public data. No API keys, credentials, or account-specific data
are ever exposed in this file or any public page.

## Airlock (second product)

Airlock is a guard that sits between an AI agent and untrusted content. Two
directions:

- **Inbound.** Text is normalised first -- Unicode tag-block characters
  decoded, invisible characters stripped, HTML comments and hidden elements
  extracted, spaced-out obfuscation collapsed -- then scored against 30
  weighted rules across 8 attack families (instruction override, role
  hijack, delimiter break, exfiltration, tool abuse, authority spoof, memory
  poison, encoding). Scores combine with noisy-OR rather than addition, so
  several weak signals cannot sum to false certainty. Block at 0.75, flag at
  0.40.
- **Outbound.** Destination checked against an allowlist; payload checked
  against 11 credential patterns (AWS access key and secret, Anthropic,
  OpenAI, GitHub, Slack, Google, Stripe, private keys, JWTs, bearer tokens)
  and 7 personal-data patterns (email, E.164 phone, credit card, SSN,
  Aadhaar, PAN, IBAN), plus a query-string entropy check.

Audit: one append-only entry per decision, holding a SHA-256 of the scanned
content, its byte count, the verdict, the rules that fired and a redacted
excerpt. The raw content is not stored. Append-only is enforced by a
Postgres trigger that rejects UPDATE and DELETE on the table, not by
application code. Exportable as CSV. The guard fails closed: if it cannot
decide, the response is an error and the verdict is block.

**Status, stated precisely because it is the thing most likely to be
misreported:** the code is written (FastAPI + Postgres backend, Next.js
dashboard, Python and TypeScript SDKs) and the detector runs locally under
Docker Compose. It is NOT hosted. There is no callable endpoint, no
metering, no billing, no price and nothing to buy. The only Airlock action
available on this site is joining the early-access list at
https://www.nanoneuron.ai/airlock.

**On accuracy claims:** the repository contains an 18-case suite written by
us -- 11 attacks (including payloads hidden in Unicode tag characters, HTML
comments and spaced text) and 7 benign documents. On the current rules it
blocks all 11 and scores all 7 benign documents at 0.00. That is a smoke
test on self-authored cases, not a benchmark, and it must not be reported as
a precision, recall or accuracy figure. No benchmark has been published. The
stated next step is seeding the corpus from public injection datasets and
publishing both the corpus and the results, including the misses.

## Commercial scope

Active MVP under continued single-developer development, not a finished
commercial product with support SLAs. Capabilities described here reflect
what is actually implemented and, where noted, actually verified live, as of
the review date above — re-verify against the running product if this file
is more than a few weeks old.
